title: Ali's letter to Malik al-Ashtar
hook: people are either your brother in faith or your equal in creation
tomorrow: can an email be fair? a ruler's letters say yes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Umar's letter: equal before you, in a courtroom. Today, another letter makes the circle wider.

The cashier, the driver, the voice on the support line: strangers you may never see again, who still hear your tone on your worst day. Nothing ties you to them: no family, no team, maybe no shared faith. So what is a stranger to you? Ali, the Prophet's cousin, answered in a letter to the man he sent to govern Egypt, Malik al-Ashtar.
screen: `THE CASHIER. THE DRIVER.` → `WHAT IS A STRANGER TO YOU?`

segments.voice: The letter is kept in Nahj al-Balagha, a collection of Ali's sermons and letters. Fill your heart with mercy for the people, he tells Malik, with love for them and kindness toward them. Don't be a predator over them. For people are of two kinds: either your brother in faith, or your equal in creation. They will slip and make mistakes, so forgive them as you'd want God to forgive you. Faith is one bond, and a real one. It isn't the only one. Everyone under Malik's rule, sharing his faith or not, is owed the same mercy, because the same God made them. Here's a neighbor who asks it as a question. In the Hebrew Bible, read by Jews and Christians, the prophet Malachi says: “Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?” Shared ground: both root the bond between people in one Creator. One honest difference: readers of Malachi differ on whether the father there is God or an ancestor, and the prophet is calling his own people to keep faith with each other. Muslims don't call God father, and Ali writes an order to a governor about how power treats everyone. Two voices, one question, neither needing to become the other.

notes: Unity thread (wisdom day): neighbor = Malachi 2:10 (KJV), read by Jews and Christians. Shared: one Creator behind the human bond. Honest difference: readers differ on whether Malachi's 'one father' is God or an ancestor (Abraham/Jacob), and the prophet addresses his own people's faithlessness to each other; Muslims don't call God father, and Ali's line is a governor's instruction covering people outside the faith. Confirm a Jewish and a Christian reader find this fair and unranked.
